outlines.version: Skills measured as of October 7, 2026 (page updated 2026-10-21)

domains.title: Develop AI solutions by using Azure data management services
domains.weight: 30–35% at a glance (body heading still 25–30%; change log says increased)

domains.title: Connect to and consume Azure services

articles.title: .NET and C#: Platform, Runtime and Language Trade-offs
articles.scope: Compares .NET Framework, modern .NET and .NET Standard and the support model in late 2026 (.NET 8 and 9 end 2026-11-10; .NET 10 LTS to 2028-11-14; .NET 11 STS, due November 2026, also ends November 2028). Covers value vs reference types, records vs classes vs structs, C# 14 extension members and C# 15 union types and closed hierarchies, JIT with dynamic PGO vs ReadyToRun vs Native AOT, GC modes including DATAS, and Span<T>/pooling measured with BenchmarkDotNet. Afterwards the reader can pick a target framework, compilation mode and upgrade path backed by measurements.

articles.title: Python for C# Engineers: Typing, Data Models, Async, Packaging and Performance
articles.scope: Maps C# habits onto Python: gradual typing and Protocols vs nominal interfaces, dataclasses and Pydantic vs records, context managers vs IDisposable, generators vs IEnumerable, decorators vs attributes, exceptions, and the GIL vs the free-threaded build (supported since 3.14). Covers Python 3.15 changes (PEP 810 lazy imports, PEP 799 profiling package, UTF-8 default). Afterwards the reader writes idiomatic Python for the AI-200 and agentic-AI code samples.

articles.title: Async and Concurrency: .NET Tasks vs Python asyncio
articles.scope: Covers async/await state machines, the thread pool and sync-over-async starvation, Task.Run vs async I/O, ConfigureAwait, ValueTask and IAsyncEnumerable, cancellation, and lock/System.Threading.Lock, SemaphoreSlim, Interlocked and bounded Channel<T>. Maps each idea to asyncio (event loop, TaskGroup structured concurrency, cancellation), threads vs processes and the free-threaded build. Afterwards the reader can diagnose starvation and choose the right primitive in either language.

articles.title: Building HTTP Services: ASP.NET Core vs FastAPI
articles.scope: Builds one service in both stacks: generic host and Kestrel vs ASGI on Uvicorn, Minimal APIs vs controllers vs FastAPI routers, DI lifetimes vs FastAPI dependencies, built-in .NET 10 validation vs Pydantic, RFC 9457 Problem Details and deliberate status codes, OpenAPI 3.1 generation, and health/readiness endpoints. Covers statelessness for scale-out: externalized session state, sharing the Data Protection key ring, when sticky sessions are unavoidable, and graceful shutdown. Probe semantics live in devops/kubernetes.

articles.title: Outbound HTTP and SDK Clients: Client Lifetime, Connection Pooling and Socket Exhaustion
articles.scope: Contrasts IHttpClientFactory with a long-lived SocketsHttpHandler and PooledConnectionLifetime, socket exhaustion, DNS refresh and HTTP/2 connection limits, with httpx.AsyncClient lifespans in FastAPI. Shows thread-safe singleton Azure SDK and AWS SDK/boto3 clients, credential reuse, and client reuse across Lambda and Functions invocations. The SDK programming-model comparison lives in cloud/compare.

articles.title: Resilient Outbound Calls: Timeouts, Retries, Circuit Breakers and Hedging
articles.scope: Implements timeouts and deadline propagation, retries with exponential backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, hedging, bulkheads and client-side rate limiters with Polly v8 and Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience, and tenacity or stamina with httpx. Explains idempotency requirements, retry amplification across layers, SDK retry modes, and handling LLM-provider throttling (tokens-per-minute quotas, 429 with Retry-After). Pattern theory stays in architecture/patterns and architecture/reliability.
articles.boundary: Code-level implementation in .NET (Polly, Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience) and Python (tenacity); the pattern lives in retry-timeout-circuit-breaker-bulkhead.

articles.title: Configuration, Secrets and Feature Flags in Application Code
articles.scope: Covers layered configuration and IOptions vs IOptionsSnapshot vs IOptionsMonitor vs pydantic-settings, per-environment configuration, Key Vault references and Secrets Manager caching clients, dual-secret rotation without downtime, Microsoft.FeatureManagement and OpenFeature flags, and log redaction with Microsoft.Extensions.Compliance.Redaction and structlog processors. Key Vault, App Configuration, Secrets Manager and AppConfig depth stays in the provider folders.

articles.title: Background Work and Graceful Shutdown: Hosted Services, Schedulers and Task Queues (.NET vs Python)
articles.scope: Compares BackgroundService/Worker Service, Quartz.NET and Hangfire with Celery, Dramatiq and arq; singleton jobs guarded by distributed locks; and SIGTERM draining (HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout, Uvicorn lifespan) within container, Container Apps revision and Lambda shutdown budgets. Shows when Functions or Lambda timers and queue triggers replace an in-process worker, and how queue-driven workers scale on lag with KEDA.

articles.title: Packaging Services: dotnet publish Modes and SDK Container Images vs Python Wheels, Lockfiles and Images
articles.scope: Compares framework-dependent, self-contained, single-file, ReadyToRun and Native AOT builds; dotnet publish /t:PublishContainer with chiseled images; and uv, pyproject.toml, PEP 751 pylock.toml and manylinux wheels for Lambda zip, layer and container-image packages. Covers dependency management inside the package, image tags for approved versions, and SBOMs (linking security/supply-chain). Registry and deployment depth live in cloud/azure/containers, cloud/aws/iac-devops and devops/.

articles.title: Diagnosing .NET and Python Services: Profilers, Dumps, Counters and Traces
articles.scope: Uses dotnet-counters, dotnet-trace, dotnet-dump, dotnet-gcdump and dotnet-monitor to find thread-pool starvation, lock contention and GC/LOH pressure, and py-spy, memray, tracemalloc, asyncio debug mode and Python 3.15's Tachyon sampling profiler for Python. Shows how to read logs for bottlenecks and debug service-integration failures; OpenTelemetry, KQL and CloudWatch depth live in devops/observability and the provider folders.

articles.title: Testing Distributed Services: Unit, Integration, Contract and Event-Driven Tests
articles.scope: Contrasts test doubles with in-memory hosts (WebApplicationFactory, FastAPI TestClient), Testcontainers dependencies, HTTP mocks (WireMock.Net, respx) and consumer-driven contract tests (Pact). Shows how to test asynchronous flows (eventual assertions, outbox relays, idempotent consumers, poison messages) with xUnit v3 and pytest, plus Aspire app tests. Pipeline execution lives in devops/ci-cd; emulator depth in the provider iac-devops folders.

articles.title: Case Study: Upgrading from .NET 9 and Angular 20 to .NET 10 LTS and Angular 22
articles.scope: Walks through the upgrade forced by .NET 9 (2026-11-10) and Angular 20 LTS (2026-11-28) leaving support: .NET 10 LTS vs .NET 11 STS, the stepwise ng update 20 to 21 to 22 with TypeScript 5.8/5.9 to 6.0, TypeScript 6.0 default changes as upgrade work, and why TypeScript 7 waits (Angular 22 accepts only TypeScript 6.0.x). Afterwards the reader has a tested upgrade plan with rollback points.

articles.title: REST vs gRPC (and Where GraphQL Fits)
articles.scope: Compares REST/JSON with gRPC/Protobuf on payload cost, streaming modes, deadlines, HTTP/2 multiplexing and the L7 load-balancing problem, HTTP/3, and browser reach via gRPC-Web and JSON transcoding; adds GraphQL (typed schema, N+1 resolvers, caching, subscriptions). Shows where a BFF or gateway changes the choice, linking API Management, API Gateway and AppSync in the provider folders.

articles.title: API Versioning and Contract Evolution
articles.scope: Classifies breaking vs non-breaking changes across OpenAPI 3.1/3.2, Protobuf and GraphQL, compares URI, query, header and media-type versioning (Asp.Versioning, FastAPI routers), design-first vs code-first (TypeSpec, Kiota/NSwag), expand/contract, and Deprecation (RFC 9745) and Sunset (RFC 8594) headers. Relates code versions to API Management versions/revisions and API Gateway stages.

articles.title: Pagination: Offset vs Keyset vs Cursor
articles.scope: Compares offset, keyset and opaque-cursor pagination on cost, index needs and stability, with PostgreSQL and SQL Server SQL; shows Cosmos DB continuation tokens and DynamoDB LastEvaluatedKey; and designs Link-header (RFC 8288) or envelope contracts with filters and counts that avoid full scans.

articles.title: Idempotent APIs: Idempotency Keys, Conditional Requests and Safe Retries
articles.scope: Starts from RFC 9110 safe/idempotent semantics and QUERY (RFC 10008), then implements the draft Idempotency-Key header (fingerprints, response store in PostgreSQL or Redis, 409/422 cases, expiry) and contrasts it with ETag/If-Match concurrency and natural upserts. Links delivery-semantics and the Powertools for AWS Lambda idempotency utility.

articles.title: Rate Limiting and Throttling: Fixed Window vs Sliding Window vs Token Bucket
articles.scope: Compares fixed-window, sliding-window, token-bucket, GCRA and concurrency limiters and where each is enforced; implements ASP.NET Core partitioned limiters, a Redis-backed distributed limiter and a FastAPI equivalent; returns 429 with Retry-After and the draft RateLimit headers; and adds client-side throttling. Gateway quotas and usage plans live in the provider folders.

articles.title: Securing HTTP APIs: Bearer Tokens, Scopes and Fine-Grained Authorization
articles.scope: Implements JWT bearer validation, scopes and claims, policy- and resource-based authorization, per-tenant checks, service-to-service auth with client credentials or managed identities/IAM roles, browser clients via BFF cookies vs SPA tokens, CORS, and keeping tokens and PII out of logs. OAuth/OIDC concepts stay in security/iam; Entra ID and Cognito in provider folders.

articles.title: Webhooks: Delivery, Signing, Verification and Retries
articles.scope: Designs both sides of webhooks: HMAC signatures and the Standard Webhooks spec, timestamp tolerance and replay protection, idempotent receivers, the Event Grid validation handshake, outbound retries with a DLQ, and SSRF controls on delivery targets; links EventBridge API destinations and Event Grid webhook handlers in the provider folders.

articles.title: HTTP Semantics Reference for API Engineers
articles.scope: Lookup tables for method properties (including QUERY), status codes (401 vs 403, 409 vs 412, PUT vs PATCH) and the header families the API articles use: Cache-Control and validators, conditional requests, content negotiation, Problem Details, Retry-After and RateLimit, Idempotency-Key, Deprecation/Sunset and traceparent, each linked to its RFC or draft.

articles.title: SignalR vs WebSockets vs Server-Sent Events vs Long Polling
articles.scope: Compares SignalR hubs (negotiation, JSON vs MessagePack, groups, stateful reconnect) with raw WebSockets, SSE, long polling and WebTransport (Baseline 2026), and covers scale-out (Redis backplane with sticky sessions vs Azure SignalR Service without them), connection limits and idle timeouts. Lists managed options (Azure SignalR Service, Web PubSub, API Gateway WebSocket APIs, AppSync Events) with depth in provider folders.

articles.title: Streaming HTTP Responses: SSE, NDJSON and Token Streams
articles.scope: Implements SSE framing with Last-Event-ID resumption, ASP.NET Core 10 TypedResults.ServerSentEvents, IAsyncEnumerable JSON and NDJSON streaming, and FastAPI StreamingResponse, consumed by EventSource or fetch with ReadableStream. Covers proxy buffering, HTTP/1.1 connection limits, cancellation and backpressure, and contrasts LLM token streams and MCP 2026-07-28's request-scoped, non-resumable SSE with EventSource resumption (transport depth in ai/protocols).

articles.title: Event-Driven vs Request-Response
articles.scope: Short decision tables on coupling, latency, failure isolation and consistency (theory linked to architecture/), then code in .NET and Python: request-reply over a broker, async request-reply (202 plus status), fan-out, and commands vs events. Workflow engines (Azure Durable Functions, AWS Step Functions, Lambda durable functions, Temporal) are linked to durable-execution-workflows.

articles.title: Queues vs Topics vs Event Streams
articles.scope: Separates point-to-point queues (competing consumers, leases), topics (fan-out, subscription filters) and partitioned logs (retention, replay, offsets, consumer groups); compares ordering (keys, sessions, FIFO groups), deduplication windows and consumer lag as the scaling signal (KEDA, Lambda iterator age). Maps models to RabbitMQ, Kafka, Redis Streams, Service Bus, Event Grid, Event Hubs, SQS, SNS, EventBridge and Kinesis.

articles.title: Redis Streams vs Apache Kafka
articles.scope: Compares Redis Streams (XADD/XREADGROUP/XACK, pending entries list and XAUTOCLAIM, MAXLEN/MINID trimming, 8.2 group-aware deletion, 8.6 idempotent production, 8.8 XNACK) with Kafka 4.x (KRaft only, replicated partitions, compaction, tiered storage, transactions, KIP-848, share groups production-ready since 4.2). Covers durability, replay, rebalances, cost and licensing (Redis 8 tri-licence incl. AGPLv3 vs BSD Valkey).

articles.title: RabbitMQ and AMQP: Exchanges, Quorum Queues and Streams (AMQP 0-9-1 vs AMQP 1.0)
articles.scope: Explains exchanges and bindings, classic vs quorum queues, RabbitMQ streams, publisher confirms and consumer acks, and how AMQP 0-9-1 differs from AMQP 1.0 links and settlement, which Azure Service Bus uses (peek-lock vs receive-and-delete). Shows MassTransit and NServiceBus topologies and links Amazon MQ in cloud/aws.

articles.title: At-Most-Once, At-Least-Once and Exactly-Once Delivery
articles.scope: Traces where losses and duplicates come from (producer retries, crash before ack, lease expiry, rebalances), contrasts Kafka transactional exactly-once with effectively-once processing, implements inbox tables and Redis SET NX dedup, and evaluates SQS FIFO deduplication, Service Bus duplicate detection and Redis idempotent production with their windows.

articles.title: Transactional Outbox vs Dual-Write (and Change Data Capture)
articles.scope: Shows why dual-write fails and implements an outbox on PostgreSQL with EF Core/Npgsql and SQLAlchemy; compares polling relays (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) with log-based CDC (logical decoding, Debezium outbox router) and managed change feeds; covers ordering, relay duplicates and table/slot growth, and library licensing (MassTransit commercial from v9, Wolverine, NServiceBus, CAP).

articles.title: Consuming Change Data Streams: Logical Decoding, Debezium and Change-Feed Processors
articles.scope: Implements consumers for PostgreSQL logical decoding and Debezium, the Cosmos DB change feed processor (leases, checkpoints, latest-version vs all-versions-and-deletes modes) and DynamoDB Streams with Lambda: per-partition ordering, replay, slot WAL retention and PG17 failover slots, delete handling and idempotent handlers.

articles.title: Consumer Failure Handling: Retries, Backoff, Dead-Letter Queues and Poison Messages
articles.scope: Classifies transient, poison and business failures and compares in-process retries, delayed retry topics, redelivery limits and DLQs with redrive, including ordering and head-of-line effects. Implements Redis Streams (XPENDING, XAUTOCLAIM, XNACK) and Kafka (retry/DLQ topics, Streams DLQ handlers from KIP-1034, share-group RENEW acks from KIP-1222), mapped to Service Bus, Event Grid, SQS redrive and Lambda destinations.

articles.title: Stream Processing: Windows, Event Time, Watermarks and Stateful Operators
articles.scope: Teaches tumbling, hopping, sliding and session windows, event time vs processing time, watermarks, late data and grace periods, and exactly-once state, comparing Kafka Streams with Flink and tick-to-OHLCV aggregation in a stream vs TimescaleDB continuous aggregates. Links Lambda with Kinesis, Azure Stream Analytics, Fabric eventstreams and Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink.

articles.title: Event Sourcing in Practice: Marten on PostgreSQL vs KurrentDB
articles.scope: Implements event-sourced order and execution lifecycles with Marten and KurrentDB (formerly EventStoreDB): streams, optimistic appends, projections, snapshots, upcasting and GDPR crypto-shredding. Theory stays in architecture/patterns.

articles.title: Building a Modular Monolith in .NET (and Extracting Services)
articles.scope: Implements module boundaries (projects, internal visibility, architecture tests, schema-per-module) and in-process messaging (direct calls, mediator, in-memory bus; MediatR commercial from v13), then extracts a service through the outbox, contrasting local transactions with sagas. The microservices-vs-modular-monolith decision lives in architecture/practice.

articles.title: Broker and Exchange Integrations: REST/WebSocket APIs vs FIX
articles.scope: Compares vendor REST and WebSocket APIs with FIX: 4.4 and 5.0 SP2 over FIXT 1.1 as venues deploy them, FIX Latest as the current standard, FIXP with SBE as the binary path, and FIX Orchestra rules of engagement. Covers feed handling (snapshot plus delta, gap detection, book rebuild, conflation), rate-limit-aware clients and an anti-corruption layer with QuickFIX/n and Python.

articles.title: Relational Modelling and Engines: PostgreSQL vs SQL Server
articles.scope: Covers normalization vs denormalization, keys (UUIDv7 vs identity), types, JSON vs relational columns, indexing (B-tree, clustered vs heap, covering, partial, expression, GIN/GiST) and execution plans; compares PostgreSQL 18 (MVCC heap, VACUUM, uuidv7(), B-tree skip scan, async I/O; 19 at RC) with SQL Server 2025 (clustered indexes, RCSI, optimized locking, JSON and vector types).

articles.title: Transaction Isolation and Concurrency Control
articles.scope: Defines anomalies (dirty and non-repeatable reads, phantoms, lost updates, read and write skew) and what each level prevents in PostgreSQL (MVCC, SSI) and SQL Server (locking RC, RCSI, snapshot). Compares optimistic control (xmin, rowversion, EF Core tokens, Cosmos DB _etag with If-Match, DynamoDB condition expressions and version attributes) with pessimistic locks, SKIP LOCKED, advisory locks and transactional batches/TransactWriteItems.

articles.title: Data Access in .NET and Python: EF Core vs Dapper vs Drivers, Pooling and Migrations
articles.scope: Compares EF Core 10, SQLAlchemy 2.0, Dapper, Npgsql and psycopg 3; client pools vs PgBouncer session/transaction pooling and Lambda connection management; passwordless Entra ID and IAM database auth with token refresh in pools; TLS verify-full and least-privilege roles; injection-safe raw SQL; enabling extensions via azure.extensions; and expand/contract migrations (EF Core, Flyway, DbUp, Alembic).

articles.title: Replication and Read Scaling from the Application Side
articles.scope: Covers read/write splitting, replica lag and read-your-writes, Npgsql multi-host Target Session Attributes and libpq target_session_attrs, and retry on failover; provider replica features are linked to the provider folders.

articles.title: Multi-Tenant Data Isolation: Row-Level Security vs Schema-per-Tenant vs Database-per-Tenant
articles.scope: Compares tenancy models on isolation, noisy neighbours, cost and per-tenant restore, and implements PostgreSQL RLS safely (SET LOCAL or set_config(..., true) under transaction pooling, FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, non-owner role), SQL Server RLS, EF Core named query filters, tenant-scoped cache keys and cross-tenant leak tests. SaaS strategy lives in architecture/.

articles.title: Time-Series and Financial Schemas: Ticks, Bars and Order Books
articles.scope: Designs schemas for ticks, OHLCV bars and order-book snapshots and deltas, bitemporal corrections, timestamp precision and numeric types (numeric/decimal vs double, JavaScript precision). Compares TimescaleDB with InfluxDB 3, QuestDB, ClickHouse and kdb+, and managed options (Azure Data Explorer, Fabric Eventhouse, Amazon Timestream for InfluxDB; Timestream for LiveAnalytics closed to new customers since 2025-06-20).

articles.title: TimescaleDB Internals: Hypertables, Chunks, Columnstore and Continuous Aggregates
articles.scope: Explains chunking, chunk_time_interval and exclusion, the rowstore/columnstore engine, continuous aggregates and jobs, using an edition matrix: Apache-2 (hypertables, time_bucket, drop_chunks), Community/TSL (columnstore, continuous aggregates, add_retention_policy, jobs, SkipScan) and Tiger Cloud only (tiered storage). Shows what Azure Database for PostgreSQL users can still do (hypertables, time_bucket, drop_chunks via pg_cron).

articles.title: Row-Oriented vs Columnar Storage
articles.scope: Explains why layout decides query cost: row stores for OLTP, column stores with dictionary, RLE, delta and XOR encodings, vectorized execution and late materialization for OLAP. Compares TimescaleDB columnstore, SQL Server columnstore, Citus columnar and DuckDB over Parquet, and when to move analytics to Fabric, Redshift or Athena.

articles.title: Indexing and Partitioning for High-Frequency Data
articles.scope: Compares time-range and hash/list partitioning, pg_partman vs hypertables, partition pruning, B-tree vs BRIN, composite (symbol, time) indexes with PostgreSQL 18 skip scan vs TimescaleDB SkipScan, write amplification vs LSM engines, bulk ingest with COPY, hot partitions and retention, verified with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS).

articles.title: Caching Strategies: Cache-Aside, Read-Through, Write-Through, Write-Behind and HTTP Caching
articles.scope: Compares cache placement and patterns, TTL, eviction, invalidation and stampede protection; implements IMemoryCache, IDistributedCache, HybridCache, output caching vs response caching and redis-py; and designs HTTP caching (no-cache vs no-store, max-age vs s-maxage, ETag, Vary) and cache keys across CloudFront cache policies and Front Door rules.

articles.title: Redis in Depth: Data Structures, Persistence, Clustering and the Valkey Split
articles.scope: Covers Redis types including streams, JSON, Query Engine, time series, probabilistic structures and vector sets; Pub/Sub vs Streams vs lists; MULTI/EXEC, Lua and functions; RDB vs AOF; cluster hash slots and hash tags; eviction and sizing; and licensing (BSD to 7.2, Valkey fork, Redis 8 tri-licence) shaping managed choices (Azure Managed Redis on Redis Enterprise 7.4.x; ElastiCache on Valkey or Redis OSS).

articles.title: Document and Key-Value Modelling: Access Patterns, Partition Keys, Query vs Scan
articles.scope: Teaches access-pattern-first modelling: high-cardinality and hierarchical partition keys, sort keys, embedding vs referencing, single-table design, secondary indexes (DynamoDB GSIs/LSIs, Cosmos DB global secondary indexes with their RU surcharge), query vs scan vs fan-out, TTL, indexing policies, and strong vs eventual reads with RU cost. Feature-by-feature comparison lives in cloud/compare.

articles.title: Vector Search in Operational Databases: pgvector, Redis, Cosmos DB and SQL
articles.scope: Implements pgvector 0.8 (types, operators, HNSW vs IVFFlat, iterative scans, memory sizing, azure.extensions allow-list), DiskANN-style indexes (pg_diskann, pgvectorscale), and Redis FLAT, HNSW and SVS-VAMANA (8.2+) with FT.HYBRID (8.4+), plus comparison rows for Cosmos DB (flat, quantizedFlat, diskANN) and SQL DiskANN indexes. Includes a managed-host table: Azure Managed Redis 7.4.x without search on Flash Optimized, ElastiCache for Valkey vector search.

articles.title: Full-Text and Hybrid Search: PostgreSQL FTS vs OpenSearch vs Redis Query Engine
articles.scope: Contrasts inverted indexes, analyzers and BM25 in OpenSearch and Redis with PostgreSQL tsvector/GIN and ts_rank (not BM25), and fuses lexical and vector results with RRF or linear scoring (Redis FT.HYBRID, Cosmos DB hybrid search linked). RAG design stays in ai/applied; Azure AI Search in ai/platforms.

articles.title: Angular Architecture: Components, DI, Routing, Forms and Rendering Modes
articles.scope: Covers standalone components vs NgModules, @if/@for/@defer, signal inputs and model, inject(), routing, forms (reactive vs template-driven vs Signal Forms, stable since v22.0), functional interceptors and CSR/SSR/prerender/incremental hydration. Upgrade notes: Angular 22 requires TypeScript 6.0.x (TypeScript 7 not supported), OnPush is the default, Vitest is the default runner, and the path steps 20 to 21 to 22.

articles.title: Angular Change Detection: Zone.js vs Zoneless, Eager vs OnPush, and Signals
articles.scope: Explains Zone.js tree checks vs zoneless scheduling (default since v21) and Eager vs OnPush (OnPush default since v22; Default deprecated as an alias of Eager), signals (computed, effect, linkedSignal, resource, httpResource), effect pitfalls, interop with RxJS and measuring re-render cost with Angular DevTools.

articles.title: RxJS for Angular: Observables, Subjects, Multicasting and Higher-Order Operators
articles.scope: Teaches the Observable contract, cold vs hot, Subject variants, share/shareReplay and the refCount trap, switchMap vs mergeMap vs concatMap vs exhaustMap with the failure each causes when misused, retry with backoff, rate-shaping operators, takeUntilDestroyed, and when a signal should replace a stream.

articles.title: State Management in Angular: Signal Services vs NgRx SignalStore vs NgRx Store
articles.scope: Decides where state belongs (component, signal service, SignalStore, Redux-style Store) by team size, cross-cutting needs, devtools and testability; covers source vs derived state, normalized entities, server state vs client state (httpResource, TanStack Query) and optimistic updates with rollback.

articles.title: Securing Angular Apps: Sanitization, CSP, Trusted Types, XSRF and OIDC Sign-In
articles.scope: Covers DomSanitizer and bypassSecurityTrust risks, autoCsp hash-based CSP, Trusted Types, HttpClient XSRF, CORS, token storage, and OIDC client libraries vs a BFF cookie session. Concepts stay in security/appsec and security/iam.

articles.title: Testing Angular Apps: Vitest, TestBed, Component Harnesses and Playwright
articles.scope: Migrates from Karma/Jasmine to Vitest, tests signals and zoneless components (flushing effects, fixture.whenStable), uses CDK component harnesses and HTTP testing, and adds Playwright end-to-end tests.

articles.title: TypeScript Type-System Trade-offs
articles.scope: Covers interface vs type, structural typing and branded types, strict (default since 6.0), noUncheckedIndexedAccess, unknown vs any, narrowing, discriminated unions, mapped and conditional types, runtime validation, and the 6.0 (2026-03-23) to 7.0 (2026-07-08) transition: removed options, no API in 7.0, a new API in the 7.1 beta (2026-10-20), and tools that still need 6.x.

articles.title: TypeScript vs C#: A Difference Map for .NET Engineers
articles.scope: Maps C# onto TypeScript: nominal vs structural, reified vs erased generics, nullable reference types vs strictNullChecks, enums vs literal unions, TypeScript discriminated unions vs C# 15 unions and closed hierarchies, Task vs Promise, LINQ vs array methods, attributes vs decorators, decimal vs number, and sharing contracts via OpenAPI-generated clients.

articles.title: Rendering High-Frequency Streams in the Browser
articles.scope: Compares framework, direct-DOM and canvas/WebGL rendering and covers frame batching, sampling and per-key conflation, virtual scrolling, OnPush and signals, Web Workers with OffscreenCanvas, backpressure policies, leak prevention and measuring INP.

articles.title: Real-Time Clients in Angular: SignalR, WebSocket and SSE Connection Lifecycles
articles.scope: Wraps the SignalR client, RxJS webSocket and EventSource/fetch SSE as Observables or signals with connection state machines, reconnect with jittered backoff, token refresh, gap recovery via sequence numbers and snapshot-then-delta, heartbeats and multiplexing.

articles.title: OpenAPI, API-First Design and Contract Testing in ASP.NET Core and FastAPI
articles.scope: Wave 2. Specs: OpenAPI 3.1 (JSON Schema alignment) and 3.2, design-first vs code-first, TypeSpec, and Spectral linting. Generation: built-in OpenAPI documents in .NET 10 (Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi, 3.1) vs FastAPI's generated docs, and client generation with Kiota and openapi-generator. Contract tests: consumer-driven (Pact) vs provider and schema-based (Schemathesis), and breaking-change detection with oasdiff in CI. Gateways: importing into API Management and API Center vs API Gateway. Agents: OpenAPI as the agent tool contract for the Foundry OpenAPI tool and AgentCore Gateway targets (AIP-C01 2.5.2). It complements api-versioning-and-evolution.

articles.title: GraphQL vs REST vs gRPC: HotChocolate, Strawberry, AppSync and API Management GraphQL
articles.scope: Wave 2. Adds GraphQL to the existing rest-vs-grpc-apis article, which it links rather than repeats. GraphQL topics: schema-first vs code-first, resolvers, the N+1 problem and DataLoader, persisted queries, subscriptions, federation (Apollo Federation, HotChocolate Fusion), and security (depth and complexity limits, introspection, authorisation per field). Implementations are HotChocolate in C# and Strawberry in Python. Managed options are AWS AppSync (JS resolvers, pipeline resolvers, merged APIs, AppSync Events) and API Management GraphQL (pass-through vs synthetic with resolvers). A decision table covers caching, tooling, browser reach and streaming.

articles.title: Aspire for Distributed .NET and Python: AppHost, Service Defaults, Dashboard and Publishing to Container Apps and AWS
articles.scope: Wave 2. Covers Aspire 13.x (renamed from .NET Aspire in November 2025, with Python first-class and uv support, and a TypeScript AppHost in 13.2). AppHost: resources, WithReference and WaitFor, parameters and secrets, and integrations (PostgreSQL/TimescaleDB, Redis, Kafka, Azure and AWS resources). Python resources run uvicorn and FastAPI apps. Service defaults: OpenTelemetry, health checks, resilience and service discovery, with the dashboard. Tooling: the aspire CLI, and aspire publish and deploy to Azure Container Apps (with azd), Docker Compose or Kubernetes. AWS: provisioning through Aspire.Hosting.AWS (CloudFormation/CDK, Lambda); check maturity before relying on it. Testing uses Aspire.Hosting.Testing. It links to opentelemetry-in-practice and testing-distributed-services.

articles.title: Agent UI Patterns in Angular: Streaming Chat, AG-UI Events, Tool Approval, Generative UI and Citations
articles.scope: Wave 3. Streaming: tokens over SSE or fetch streams into signals, with cancellation and backpressure. Events: AG-UI events (run lifecycle, text message content, tool call start, args and end, state snapshot and delta) mapped to components. Human in the loop: tool-approval and interrupt dialogs, overrides and edge-case escalation (AI-500 2.4.2, AI-103 2.2.5). Generative UI: AG-UI, A2UI and MCP Apps. Trust: citations and provenance display. Error, latency and partial-result states, accessibility (aria-live), and HAX guideline checks (AI-500 1.1.6). Backends shown are Microsoft Agent Framework and Strands. It links to frontend/realtime/real-time-ui-streaming and security/ai-security/human-oversight-transparency-provenance.

articles.title: Micro-Frontends and Module Federation: When to Split an Angular Estate
articles.scope: Wave 5. Decision drivers: team topology and Conway's law, vertical vs horizontal splits, and the modular-monolith alternative with Nx boundaries. Composition options: build-time packages, server-side composition, and client-side runtime composition with Module Federation 2.0, Native Federation for the Angular esbuild builder, import maps, and Web Components through Angular Elements. Runtime concerns: shared dependencies and version skew, routing, cross-app communication and state, and a shared design system. Delivery: deployment and caching on Static Web Apps or CloudFront, and performance budgets. It closes with anti-patterns and an ADR template, and links to messaging/integration/microservices-vs-modular-monoliths.

terms.definition: An application-defined lock on an arbitrary key held by the database (PostgreSQL advisory locks, SQL Server application locks) that coordinates processes without locking rows and is released with the session or transaction.
APIs exposing async data as signals: resource() reruns a loader when its reactive params change, aborting stale loads, and httpResource() wraps HttpClient so interceptors still apply.

Angular's signal-based forms API, experimental in v21 and stable since v22.0, where a form() model and schema derive each field's value, validity and state as signals bound to inputs with the FormField directive.
Angular's fine-grained reactive primitives (signal, computed, effect, linkedSignal) that track which computations and templates read them so only those update when a value changes.
A compact binary serialization format whose readers resolve data against the writer's schema, usually fetched from a schema registry, making it the common choice for evolvable Kafka payloads.
An open-source event-streaming platform storing records in partitioned, replicated, disk-based logs, which since 4.0 runs only in KRaft mode without ZooKeeper.
Exposing incompatible contract revisions side by side, selected by URI path, query string, header or media type, so existing clients keep working while new ones adopt breaking changes.
The async Python interface between servers such as Uvicorn and frameworks such as FastAPI, supporting HTTP, WebSockets and lifespan events, unlike the synchronous request-only WSGI.

Microsoft's open-source, code-first toolchain whose AppHost composes services, containers and backing resources, shows their OpenTelemetry data in a dashboard and deploys them, across C#, Python and JavaScript services.
An ASP.NET Core library for real-time hub RPC that negotiates WebSockets, SSE or long polling and supports JSON or MessagePack, groups and stateful reconnect.

Sequences whose elements arrive asynchronously and are consumed with await foreach (C# IAsyncEnumerable), async for (Python async generators) or for await (JavaScript AsyncIterable), with pull-based backpressure.
A machine-readable specification, at 3.1, for describing message-driven APIs (channels, operations, messages and broker bindings) in the way OpenAPI describes HTTP APIs.
Python's single-threaded cooperative concurrency library in which coroutines suspend at await so one loop multiplexes many I/O operations, and any blocking call stalls every task on the loop.
A guarantee that messages are retried until acknowledged, so none are lost but any may arrive more than once, making idempotent consumers mandatory.
A guarantee that each message arrives zero or one times because nothing is retried, so messages can be lost but never duplicated.
The default relational index, a balanced sorted tree that supports equality, range and ordered scans in logarithmic time and is cheapest when queries filter on its leading columns.

Backward compatibility lets new code read data from old code; forward compatibility lets old code read data from new code, usually by ignoring unknown fields; which one a change needs depends on who deploys first.
Recording both when a fact was true (valid time) and when the system learned it (recorded time), so corrections never overwrite history and past views can be reproduced exactly.
A PostgreSQL index storing summary values per range of table blocks, tiny and cheap to maintain but effective only when values correlate with physical order, as timestamps in append-only tables do.

HTTP response instructions for caches: no-store forbids storing, no-cache allows storing but requires revalidation, max-age sets freshness for all caches, and s-maxage overrides it for shared caches such as CDNs.
The rule a full cache uses to remove entries, such as Redis allkeys-lru, volatile-lfu or noeviction, which decides whether memory pressure drops data or rejects writes.
The combination of path, query strings, headers and cookies that identifies a cached response; too few parts serve the wrong content and too many destroy the hit ratio.

A CNCF-graduated specification, at 1.0.2, for a common event envelope (id, source, type, specversion plus optional attributes) with HTTP, Kafka, AMQP, MQTT and NATS bindings in structured or binary content mode.

A clustered index stores the table's rows in key order, the SQL Server default, while a heap stores rows unordered with separate indexes pointing in, the PostgreSQL model, which changes key choice and insert patterns.
A cold observable starts a new producer per subscriber, such as one HTTP request each, while a hot observable shares one producer so late subscribers miss earlier values.
A layout that stores each column contiguously so analytic queries read only needed columns and compress well, at the cost of slower single-row writes and lookups.

Concurrency is structuring many tasks with overlapping lifetimes to make progress, such as thousands of in-flight I/O calls on a few threads, while parallelism is executing computations simultaneously on multiple cores.
Merging superseded updates for the same key so only the latest is delivered or rendered, bounding work by the number of keys rather than the message rate.
A named set of consumers sharing a stream so each partition (Kafka, Event Hubs) or entry (Redis Streams) goes to one member at a time, while separate groups each read the full stream.
How far a consumer trails the head of a queue or stream, measured in messages, offsets or age, and the usual signal for scaling consumers with KEDA or alerting on Lambda iterator age.

A TimescaleDB Community-edition materialized view refreshed incrementally by policy for changed time buckets, optionally merging unmaterialized data at query time, commonly rolling ticks into OHLCV bars.
Testing in which each consumer records the requests and responses it relies on as a contract that the provider's build verifies, catching breaking changes without end-to-end environments.

Cancellation in which the caller only signals intent and the callee checks and stops itself: CancellationToken in .NET and AbortSignal in JavaScript are passed explicitly, while asyncio injects CancelledError at the next await.
An index that contains every column a query needs, often through INCLUDE columns, so the engine answers from the index alone without visiting the table.

terms.term: C# union types and closed hierarchies
terms.definition: C# 15 features (default for net11.0): union declares a value that is one of several case types with exhaustive switches, and closed limits derivation to the declaring assembly so switches over descendants need no default arm.
Removing or obscuring sensitive values such as tokens, secrets and PII before they reach logs, traces or responses, for example with Microsoft.Extensions.Compliance.Redaction or structlog processors.

Reusing a bounded set of open database connections across requests, in the driver (Npgsql, psycopg_pool) or in a server-side pooler such as PgBouncer or RDS Proxy that multiplexes many clients onto fewer connections.
A separate queue or topic that receives messages after they exceed a delivery limit, expire or fail validation, so they stop blocking consumers and can be inspected and redriven.

Decimal types (C# decimal, PostgreSQL numeric) represent base-10 amounts exactly, while binary doubles such as the JavaScript number cannot represent 0.1 exactly and lose integer precision above 2^53, so prices and int64 IDs need string or decimal encoding in JSON.
Template @defer blocks whose content and dependencies load lazily on a trigger such as viewport, interaction or idle, and which also scope incremental hydration.

The .NET container's sharing rules (transient per resolution, scoped per scope or request, singleton per container), where a singleton capturing a scoped service becomes a captive dependency shared across requests.
.NET's support tracks: even-numbered LTS releases get three years and odd-numbered STS releases two, so .NET 8 and 9 both end on 2026-11-10 and .NET 10 LTS runs to 2028-11-14.
Compiler plug-ins that generate C# at build time (for System.Text.Json, LoggerMessage, configuration binding and regex), replacing runtime reflection so code stays trimming- and Native AOT-safe.
The inconsistency that arises when code commits to a database and publishes to a broker as two separate operations, so a crash between them leaves one updated and the other not.
The practical outcome of at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers or deduplication: duplicates still arrive but have no additional effect.
An ETag identifies one version of a resource; clients send it in If-None-Match to revalidate a cache (304) or in If-Match so an update applies only if unchanged (otherwise 412).
Event time is when something happened at the source and processing time is when the system sees it; aggregating by event time gives reproducible results under delays and reordering.

Applying each message's effects exactly once, achievable only inside a system that controls both reads and writes, such as Kafka transactions for read-process-write, not across arbitrary external side effects.

A zero-downtime schema change made in steps (add the new structure, dual-write and backfill, switch reads, then remove the old) so old and new code versions run together during rollouts and rollbacks.

The industry standard for orders, executions and market data, whose session layer (logon, heartbeats, sequence numbers, resend and gap fill) gives ordered, recoverable delivery; FIX Latest is the maintained application layer.
A PostgreSQL inverted index mapping each element of a composite value (jsonb keys, array items, tsvector lexemes) to its rows, used for jsonb metadata filters and full-text search.

Handling SIGTERM by stopping intake, finishing or checkpointing in-flight requests and messages, and exiting within the platform's grace period, which differs from health probes that only report state.
A query language and runtime in which clients send queries, mutations or subscriptions against a typed schema, usually at one endpoint, and receive exactly the fields requested.
A CNCF RPC framework that generates clients and servers from Protocol Buffers contracts over HTTP/2, supporting unary and streaming calls with deadlines and cancellation.

Delay in which one stalled item blocks everything queued behind it, whether a lost TCP packet under HTTP/2, a slow request on an HTTP/1.1 connection, or a poison message in an ordered partition or session.
Authenticating a request by sending an HMAC of its body and a timestamp computed with a shared secret, which the receiver recomputes with a constant-time comparison to detect tampering and replays.
HTTP's binary framing (RFC 9113) that multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection with header compression, removing HTTP-level but not TCP-level head-of-line blocking.
HTTP over QUIC (RFC 9114 and RFC 9000), a UDP-based encrypted transport with independent streams, so one lost packet stalls only its own stream and connections survive network changes.
A .NET library combining an in-process L1 and optional distributed L2 cache behind GetOrCreateAsync with stampede protection and logical tag invalidation.
Attaching client state and event listeners to server-rendered HTML instead of re-rendering it, with Angular's incremental hydration deferring that work per @defer block until its trigger fires.

A TimescaleDB table partitioned automatically into time chunks (optionally also by a space column) but queried as one table, available in the Apache-2 edition that Azure Database for PostgreSQL offers.

A client-generated identifier sent with a request or message so the receiver can recognise a retry and return the original outcome instead of repeating the side effect; the HTTP header is still an IETF Internet-Draft.
A Core Web Vitals metric measuring the delay from a user interaction to the next frame painted, near the worst across a visit, which main-thread work from high-frequency updates inflates.
A search structure mapping each analyzed term to the documents containing it, which lets full-text engines such as OpenSearch and Redis answer keyword queries without scanning documents.
The concurrency effects isolation levels are defined against: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms, lost updates and read skew.

The degree to which a transaction is shielded from concurrent ones, defined by the anomalies it permits and implemented differently per engine, so the same name can behave differently in PostgreSQL and SQL Server.
The browser and Node scheduler that runs one task at a time and drains all microtasks such as promise callbacks before the next macrotask or render, so long synchronous work freezes the page.

A Kafka consumption mode, production-ready since 4.2, in which many consumers read the same partitions with per-record acknowledgement, lock renewal and redelivery, giving queue semantics beyond one consumer per partition.
Paging by filtering on the last-seen value of a unique indexed sort key, so each page is an index range scan that stays fast and stable under inserts but cannot jump to page N.
A Kafka retention mode that keeps at least the latest record per key and later drops tombstoned keys, so a topic serves as a durable changelog of current state.
PostgreSQL's mechanism for turning WAL into row-level change streams through a replication slot that retains WAL until the consumer confirms it, so an abandoned slot can fill the disk.
Emulating push by holding each HTTP request open until data arrives or a timeout passes and immediately issuing the next one, as SignalR does when WebSockets and SSE are unavailable.
A storage structure that buffers writes in memory and flushes sorted immutable files that background merges consolidate, giving high write throughput at the cost of read and space amplification.

Broker-side rejection of a message whose ID was already seen within a window, five minutes for SQS FIFO, configurable up to seven days for Service Bus, with duplicates outside the window still possible.

A time-limited exclusive claim on a received message that, if it expires unacknowledged, makes the message available again, a leading source of duplicates; Redis Streams instead keeps entries pending until claimed or (since 8.8) released.

ASP.NET Core's lambda-based endpoint model with endpoint filters, typed results and (in .NET 10) built-in validation, an alternative to MVC controllers with less ceremony and better Native AOT support.

A technique in which writers create new row versions so readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers; PostgreSQL keeps old versions in the table until VACUUM, SQL Server in a version store.
A performance bug in which code issues one query for a list and then one more per item, typical of ORM lazy loading and naive GraphQL resolvers, fixed with eager loading, joins or batching.
A .NET publishing mode that compiles an app ahead of time into a self-contained native executable without a JIT, trading reflection and dynamic-code limits for fast startup and low memory.
Newline-delimited JSON, one complete JSON value per line, used to stream records over HTTP or files without SSE's event framing or reconnection semantics.
An NgRx state container built from signals and composable features (withState, withComputed, withMethods, rxMethod, entities), lighter than the action-reducer-effect NgRx Store.
Static tracking of whether a value may be null: C# nullable reference types produce warnings and TypeScript strictNullChecks produces errors, and neither is enforced at runtime.
A per-interval summary of trades (open, high, low, close and volume) derived from tick data for charts, indicators and backtests.

A strategy that checks a component only on input reference changes, its own events, signal or async-pipe updates or explicit marks, the component default since v22, with ChangeDetectionStrategy.Eager restoring check-always.
A vendor-neutral machine-readable description format for HTTP APIs, at 3.2.1 in September 2026, used to generate documentation, clients and tests; ASP.NET Core 10 emits 3.1 by default.
Letting edits proceed without locks and rejecting a write whose version value (rowversion, xmin, ETag, _etag or a DynamoDB version attribute) changed since it was read.
Showing a user's change immediately before the server confirms it, then reconciling or rolling back when the response arrives.

The .NET binding of configuration sections to typed classes, read once with IOptions<T>, per scope with IOptionsSnapshot<T>, or live with change notifications through IOptionsMonitor<T>, which governs dynamic refresh.
The live set of resting buy and sell orders for an instrument, published as top-of-book (L1), aggregated price levels (L2) or individual orders (L3) via snapshots and incremental updates.

A key that guarantees in-order, one-at-a-time processing for messages sharing it while different keys proceed in parallel, as SQS FIFO message groups, Service Bus sessions and Kafka message keys do in different ways.
Writing a state change and its event to an outbox table in one local transaction, then relaying outbox rows to the broker by polling or CDC, so state and published events cannot diverge.

ASP.NET Core output caching stores responses on the server under app-controlled policies with tag eviction, while response caching middleware only honours HTTP cache headers set by clients and servers.
A planner optimization that skips partitions whose bounds cannot match a query's partition-key predicates, at plan time for constants and at execution time for parameters.

Connecting with short-lived tokens issued to a workload identity (Microsoft Entra ID for Azure Database for PostgreSQL, IAM authentication for RDS and Aurora) instead of stored passwords, so pools must refresh credentials.
Taking locks before modifying data, for example with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or UPDLOCK hints, so competing writers wait instead of failing, at the cost of blocking and deadlock risk.
An open-source PostgreSQL extension adding vector, halfvec, bit and sparsevec types, distance operators and HNSW and IVFFlat indexes so embeddings live beside relational data.
A message that fails every time it is processed, for example because it is malformed, so without a delivery limit it is redelivered forever and blocks ordered consumers.
PostgreSQL maintenance that reclaims dead row versions, updates the visibility map for index-only scans and freezes old transaction IDs; tables bloat and wraparound looms when it falls behind.
The RFC 9457 JSON error format (type, title, status, detail, instance plus extensions) that gives HTTP APIs a uniform machine-readable error contract.
Google's language-neutral schema language and compact binary encoding, in which numbered fields let old and new readers skip unknown fields, used by gRPC and many event payloads.
A Python library that validates and serializes data from type-annotated models at runtime, used by FastAPI for request contracts and by LLM SDKs for structured outputs.
The GIL lets only one CPython thread run bytecode at a time; the optional free-threaded build (PEP 703, officially supported since 3.14) removes it so CPU-bound threads run in parallel.
Optional annotations checked by external tools such as mypy or pyright but ignored by the interpreter, with typing.Protocol giving structural interfaces, unlike C#'s enforced nominal types.
The operator tree the optimizer chooses for a query, shown with estimated or actual rows, timings and buffer reads by EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) in PostgreSQL and actual plans in SQL Server.
A query reads only items under one partition-key value, optionally narrowed by sort-key conditions, while a scan reads the whole table and filters afterwards, so its cost grows with total data.
An open-source message broker that routes messages from exchanges to queues by bindings, with quorum queues for replicated durability and streams for replayable logs.

An isolation level in which each statement sees only data committed before it began, implemented in PostgreSQL with a per-statement snapshot and in SQL Server with shared locks unless READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT is on (the Azure SQL Database default).
A guarantee that a client always sees its own earlier writes even if other clients see stale data, provided by Cosmos DB session consistency or by routing a user's reads to the primary after writes.
Redis Cluster's 16,384 slots that keys hash into for sharding, where multi-key commands must target one slot, which hash tags such as {order:42} force.

Redis's durability options: RDB writes periodic point-in-time snapshots and can lose recent writes, while AOF logs every write and replays it on restart with fsync policies trading durability for throughput.
Redis's fire-and-forget broadcast that pushes each message to clients subscribed at that moment and stores nothing, used as the SignalR Redis backplane.

Redis's secondary indexing and search, built into Redis Open Source since 8.0, indexing hashes and JSON for text, tag, numeric, geo and vector (FLAT, HNSW, and SVS-VAMANA since 8.2) queries, with FT.HYBRID since 8.4.

Bounding a Redis stream by entry count or oldest allowed ID on XADD or XTRIM, optionally approximate, which removes old entries whether or not groups processed them unless Redis 8.2's group-aware options are used.
A Redis append-only log type with time-based IDs, range and blocking reads, consumer groups with a pending entries list, and, since Redis 8.6, idempotent production that deduplicates retried writes.

Rules acting on aging data (compress, move to cheaper storage or delete) that TimescaleDB applies per chunk: drop_chunks is Apache-2, add_retention_policy is Community and tiered object storage is Tiger Cloud only.
A PostgreSQL and SQL Server feature that attaches predicates to a table so every query sees or changes only rows the session may access, such as one tenant's rows.

Operators that map values to inner observables and flatten them: switchMap cancels the previous, mergeMap runs all concurrently, concatMap queues in order and exhaustMap ignores new values while one is active.

Observables that are also observers: Subject multicasts only new values, BehaviorSubject holds a current value, ReplaySubject replays a buffer, and AsyncSubject emits only the final value on completion.

RFC 9110 properties: safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and QUERY from RFC 10008) are read-only, idempotent methods (the safe ones plus PUT and DELETE) have the same effect however often sent, and POST and PATCH are neither by default.

An alternate key for querying a NoSQL table, either global (any partition key, eventually consistent, own capacity) or local (same partition key, different sort key); Cosmos DB's global secondary indexes are change-feed-synced read-only containers.
Using per-stream sequence numbers to spot missed or out-of-order updates and recover by resend request or snapshot reload before applying further deltas.
One-way server-to-client streaming in an ordinary HTTP response of type text/event-stream, whose EventSource API reconnects automatically and resumes with Last-Event-ID.

Server state is a cached, possibly stale copy of data owned by a backend that needs fetching, invalidation and refetching, while client state is UI-owned data such as selections; mixing them in one store causes staleness bugs.
A shared layer, such as Redis pub/sub or Azure SignalR Service as a connection proxy, that relays hub messages between server instances so broadcasts reach clients on any instance.
A FIX Trading Community binary encoding with fixed-offset fields for low-latency messages, usually carried over the FIXP session protocol instead of tag-value FIX.
Storing several entity types in one NoSQL table with overloaded generic keys so related items share a partition and each access pattern is served by one query.

A row-locking clause (PostgreSQL FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, SQL Server READPAST) that lets concurrent workers claim different pending rows without blocking, turning a table into a work queue or outbox relay.
An isolation level in which a transaction reads a snapshot taken at its start and fails on write-write conflicts, preventing lost updates and phantoms but still allowing write skew.
The second part of a composite primary key that orders items within one partition-key value, enabling range conditions such as begins_with or between in a single query.
Components that declare their own template dependencies in an imports array instead of belonging to an NgModule, the default for new Angular code.

Groupings of an unbounded stream for aggregation: tumbling windows are fixed and non-overlapping, hopping windows overlap at a fixed advance, sliding windows follow each event, and session windows close after inactivity.

A strongly consistent read returns the latest committed write, while an eventually consistent read may return stale data in exchange for lower cost, latency or higher availability, as with DynamoDB's read modes and Cosmos DB's consistency levels.
Type compatibility decided by shape rather than declared names, so in TypeScript any object with the required members satisfies an interface, unlike C#'s nominal types.

A discipline in which concurrent child tasks are scoped to a block that cannot exit until all finish, so a failure cancels siblings and errors propagate, as asyncio TaskGroup does, unlike Task.WhenAll, which leaves other tasks running.

A rule on a topic subscription that delivers only matching messages, such as SNS filter policies, Service Bus SQL and correlation rules, Event Grid filters or EventBridge patterns, cutting consumer work and cost.
Splitting one logical table into child partitions by range, list or hash so queries and maintenance such as indexing, vacuuming and detach-based retention touch only relevant partitions.
The dependency that requires both parties to be available at the same moment, present in synchronous request-response and removed by queues that let producer and consumer run at different times.
A stand-in for a real dependency in tests: a stub returns canned answers, a mock verifies interactions and a fake is a working lightweight implementation such as an in-memory repository.
Open-source libraries for .NET, Python and other languages that start real dependencies such as PostgreSQL, Redis or Kafka in disposable containers from test code.
A .NET condition in which pool threads block, typically on .Result or .Wait(), so queued work and async continuations wait for slow thread injection and latency climbs sharply.

terms.term: Throttle vs debounce vs audit vs sample
terms.definition: RxJS rate-shaping: debounce emits after a quiet period, throttle emits then ignores for a period, audit emits the latest value at each period's end and sample emits the latest at a fixed interval.
The raw, timestamped record of every trade or quote change for an instrument, the highest-resolution and highest-volume form of market data.

TimescaleDB's hybrid engine keeping recent chunks in a rowstore and converting older chunks to a compressed columnstore by segmentby and orderby, a Community (Tiger Data License) feature absent from the Apache-2 edition.
Removal of static types at compile time so they do not exist at runtime: TypeScript erases all types when emitting JavaScript, whereas C# generics are reified and visible to reflection.

TypeScript decorators are functions that run at class definition to wrap or replace members (TC39 standard or legacy experimentalDecorators, which Angular uses), whereas C# attributes are passive metadata read by reflection.
The Go port of the TypeScript compiler, released as 7.0 on 2026-07-08 with 8-12x faster full builds and 6.0's checking behaviour but no programmatic API, which arrives in 7.1 (beta 2026-10-20).

A UUID format (RFC 9562) whose leading bits are a millisecond timestamp, so keys sort roughly by creation time and avoid random-insert index fragmentation, generated by PostgreSQL 18 uuidv7() and .NET Guid.CreateVersion7().
A BSD-licensed Linux Foundation fork of Redis 7.2.4 created in 2024 after Redis left open-source licensing, offered by Amazon ElastiCache and MemoryDB alongside Redis OSS.
The functions that score vector similarity (cosine, inner product, Euclidean L2), which must match how the embedding model was trained and normalized; on unit vectors all three rank alike.
Rendering only items in or near the viewport and recycling DOM nodes on scroll, so DOM size stays constant regardless of list length or update rate.
Browser threads that run scripts off the main thread and communicate by messages, with OffscreenCanvas letting them draw, so parsing and rendering bursts do not block input.
An HTTP callback in which a provider POSTs an event to a URL the consumer registered, so receivers must verify signatures, reject replays and handle duplicate deliveries idempotently.
A protocol (RFC 6455) that upgrades an HTTP connection into a persistent full-duplex message channel, leaving routing, acknowledgement and reconnection to the application.
A browser API and protocol over HTTP/3 offering multiple reliable streams and unreliable datagrams on one connection, Baseline across major browsers in 2026.

A durability mechanism that appends every change to a sequential log flushed before data pages, so the database can replay it after a crash; in PostgreSQL it also feeds replication and logical decoding.

An anomaly in which two transactions read overlapping rows, decide on that basis and write different rows, together breaking an invariant each preserved alone; snapshot isolation allows it and serializable prevents it.
Running Angular without Zone.js so change detection runs only on explicit notifications (signal updates, template events, async pipe, markForCheck), the default since v21.

pairs.difference: At-least-once never loses but may duplicate. Exactly-once holds only inside one system controlling reads and writes, so flows with external side effects get effectively-once through idempotent consumers.
A queue hands each message to one consumer and deletes it on ack; a log retains ordered partitions that many groups replay from their own offsets.
Consumer groups give one member per partition and ordered offsets; share groups let many members read one partition with per-record acks and redelivery, trading ordering for queue-style scaling.

Redis Streams is an in-memory-first log trimmed by count or ID with explicit claiming; Kafka is a disk-first replicated log with compaction, tiered storage and transactions, winning on retention and replay at scale.
Pub/Sub pushes only to current subscribers and stores nothing; Streams persists entries that consumers acknowledge, replay and share.
AMQP 0-9-1 defines broker topology (exchanges, bindings, queues); AMQP 1.0 defines only links and settlement between peers, so routing lives in each broker's own model.
An outbox publishes deliberately designed events written with the state change; CDC emits row changes from the log, coupling consumers to table schemas unless it only relays the outbox.
Broker deduplication rejects repeats only within its window (five minutes for SQS FIFO); an idempotent consumer tolerates duplicates whenever they arrive.
A poison message is the failing input; the DLQ is where the broker parks it after the delivery limit so it stops blocking others.
Structured mode puts attributes and data in one JSON envelope; binary mode maps attributes to protocol headers and leaves the payload untouched, letting routers filter without parsing bodies.
Event-time windows give the same bars on replay but need watermarks for late data; processing-time windows are simple but change with delays.
Durable execution writes workflows as ordinary code replayed from checkpoints, which must stay deterministic; graph-based engines declare states in a DSL that is visual but less expressive.
Both read a consistent snapshot; only serializable also rejects interleavings no serial order could produce, which prevents write skew.
Optimistic control rejects stale writes and retries, cheap under low contention; pessimistic locking blocks competitors up front, at the cost of waits and deadlocks.
Same guarantee, different mechanism: PostgreSQL uses per-statement snapshots so readers never block writers, while SQL Server takes shared locks unless READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT is on.

A clustered table stores rows in key order, so random keys fragment it; a heap stores rows anywhere and indexes point in, so key choice matters less for inserts but index-only scans depend on the visibility map.
A driver pool keeps one session per connection; transaction pooling hands server connections out per transaction, so session state such as SET or advisory locks leaks or breaks.
RLS is enforced by the database for every client; EF Core filters exist only in application queries and vanish in raw SQL or other tools.

Hypertables create chunks automatically and add columnstore and continuous aggregates (Community edition); declarative partitions are core PostgreSQL, available everywhere, but need partition management.
A continuous aggregate refreshes only changed buckets and can merge recent raw rows at query time; a materialized view recomputes fully on REFRESH.

PostgreSQL 18 skip scan lets multicolumn B-tree indexes serve queries that omit the leading column; TimescaleDB SkipScan (Community edition) speeds DISTINCT ON queries by jumping between distinct values.
Offset re-reads skipped rows so deep pages slow down and shift under inserts; keyset seeks from the last key and stays fast but cannot jump to page N.
A token bucket allows bursts up to its size while capping the average; a sliding window caps requests in any rolling interval with no burst credit.
Rate limiting is a fixed policy at a boundary regardless of load; backpressure is dynamic feedback from a consumer that is actually falling behind.
An idempotency key makes a retry return the original result, solving duplicates; If-Match fails an update when the resource changed, solving lost updates.
401 means the request lacks valid credentials and should carry WWW-Authenticate; 403 means the identity is known but not allowed.
409 reports a conflict with current state, such as a duplicate or in-flight idempotency key; 412 reports that an explicit If-Match or similar precondition was false.
PUT replaces the whole representation and is idempotent; PATCH applies a partial change that is not idempotent unless the patch format makes it so.
no-cache allows storing but requires revalidation before each reuse; no-store forbids storing at all.
Output caching is server-controlled with policies and tag eviction; response caching only follows HTTP cache headers and can be bypassed by clients.
Write-through acknowledges after both cache and store update; write-behind acknowledges after the cache and flushes later, risking unflushed writes.
RDB is compact and fast to restore but loses writes since the last snapshot; AOF logs every write for better durability at the cost of size and rewrite overhead.
A TTL lock alone cannot stop a paused holder writing after expiry; a fencing token lets the resource reject the stale holder's writes.
A query reads one partition-key value narrowed by sort-key conditions; a scan reads the whole table and filters afterwards, so cost tracks total data.
A Scan reads every item; a cross-partition query is index-served on each physical partition, so its cost grows with partition count rather than item count.

HNSW gives better recall per millisecond without training but costs memory and build time; IVFFlat builds fast and small but must be built after representative data and needs higher probes for recall.
BM25 matches exact terms such as tickers and codes; vectors match meaning but miss rare tokens, so hybrid search fuses both with RRF.
Row stores make point reads and single-row writes cheap; column stores make scans and aggregates over few columns cheap and compress better.
WebSockets give full-duplex binary-capable channels with app-defined protocols; SSE is one-way push over plain HTTP with built-in reconnection and Last-Event-ID resume.
EventSource resumes a broken stream with Last-Event-ID; MCP 2026-07-28 removed resumability, so a broken response stream loses the request and the client re-issues it with a new ID.
SignalR adds negotiation, hub RPC, groups and backplane scale-out but both ends must speak its protocol; raw WebSockets work with any client but leave routing and reconnection to you.
FIX sessions guarantee ordered recovery with sequence numbers and resend requests; vendor WebSockets usually require reconnecting and reloading a snapshot after gaps.
A .NET Task starts running when created on the thread pool; a Python coroutine does nothing until awaited or scheduled as a task on the event loop.
CancellationToken is passed explicitly and checked cooperatively; asyncio cancels by injecting CancelledError at the task's next await, which code can catch and suppress.
WhenAll waits for all tasks and leaves the rest running when one fails; TaskGroup cancels siblings on the first failure and raises an ExceptionGroup.
IOptionsSnapshot recomputes options once per scope or request; IOptionsMonitor is a singleton with live values and change callbacks, usable from singletons.
Minimal APIs map lambdas with filters and suit Native AOT; controllers bring conventions, model binding and filters suited to large APIs.
EF Core tracks changes and translates LINQ, risking N+1 and opaque SQL; Dapper maps hand-written SQL to objects with full control and no tracking.
Signals hold a current value with synchronous glitch-free derivation; observables model events over time with operators for cancellation and timing.
Store centralizes state with actions, reducers and effects for traceability; SignalStore composes local or shared stores from signals with less ceremony.
Reactive forms model controls as observable-emitting objects; Signal Forms derive field value and validity as signals from a model and schema.
switchMap cancels the in-flight request on a new value, suiting typeahead; exhaustMap ignores new values until the current one completes, suiting submit buttons.
mergeMap runs inner observables concurrently and may reorder results; concatMap runs them one at a time in order.
Zone.js checks the tree after any async event; zoneless runs only on explicit notifications, so work scales with actual changes.
C# types implement interfaces by declaration and keep them at runtime; TypeScript values match by shape and the interface is erased.
TypeScript unions are structural, tagged by a property and erased; C# unions are nominal declared types with runtime case types and compiler-checked exhaustive switches.
decimal stores base-10 values exactly; number is a binary double that cannot hold 0.1 exactly or integers above 2^53, so prices and int64 IDs cross JSON as strings.
